name: Ancylostoma duodenale

taxonomy.rank_note: Reference groups can include multiple species. Protozoan higher-rank systems differ; the lineage is provided without forcing every clade into a class rank.

morphology: Egg: commonly around 60–75 × 35–40 µm, oval, colorless and thin-shelled, with cleavage-stage blastomeres and a clear space inside the shell.
Eggs may hatch in delayed stool specimens; larvae and adults require separate identification features.

transmission.detail: Eggs hatch in soil and larvae develop to infective L3, which enter the host and mature in the small intestine. A. duodenale can also be acquired orally.

life_cycle.detail: Eggs hatch in soil and larvae develop to infective L3, which enter the host and mature in the small intestine. A. duodenale can also be acquired orally.
Segmented eggs in fresh stool; larvae may occur after specimen delay.

hosts: Primarily humans are definitive hosts; no intermediate host.
distribution: Hookworm transmission occurs in tropical and subtropical regions, including Thailand. Species prevalence needs local molecular evidence; geography alone is insufficient.
clinical_significance: Intestinal blood loss can cause iron-deficiency anemia and nutritional impairment; skin penetration may cause localized irritation.
specimen: Segmented eggs in fresh stool; larvae may occur after specimen delay.
diagnostics: Wet mount or concentration at 100–400×; species resolution requires molecular or appropriately validated larval/adult identification.
differential_diagnosis: Human hookworm eggs are not reliably species-specific.
Preserve Hd/Hn/Hw as unresolved dataset codes until the original annotation dictionary is verified; do not infer species from abbreviations.
review_status: Source-compiled educational content; not independently clinically validated

annotation_guidance: Record specimen, stage, stain, objective/total magnification, pixel calibration, source image and reviewer certainty.
Native crops of 200–650 pixels do not determine biological size. Retain µm-per-pixel calibration before resizing.
Split training, validation and test data by patient/specimen; keep related crops in the same split.
Keep damaged or ambiguous objects uncertain. Molecular confirmation of a mixed specimen does not assign every pictured object a species.
